title: Choosing where vectors live: a vector database
hook: Match the storage choice to your scale, ops team and existing stack, not to whichever tool is loudest this year.
inPlainWords: A vector database stores embeddings so you can search by meaning instead of exact words. You can add this to a database you already run, use a dedicated service built for it, run a small library inside your app, or self-host a search cluster. The right one depends on your scale and who will operate it.

useCase.title: 50,000 articles need a place for their vectors
useCase.story: The help center RAG system is moving from a prototype to production. The team must decide where embeddings live: added to the database they already run, a dedicated managed service, an in-process library, or a self-hosted search engine. Each has different costs, ops burden and limits.

approaches.name: Add a vector index to the database you already run
approaches.what: Extend the relational or document store you already operate with vector search.
approaches.greatWhen: The team already runs that database, volume is moderate, and one system is simpler than adding another.
approaches.avoidWhen: Vector volume is very large or you need specialized index tuning the extension doesn't offer.
approaches.example: Vectors sit next to orders and customers, one connection, one backup.

approaches.name: A managed vector database service
approaches.what: A dedicated cloud service purpose-built for vector search.
approaches.greatWhen: Scale, uptime and index tuning matter more than avoiding a new vendor.
approaches.avoidWhen: Data cannot leave your premises, or the team has no spare capacity to run a new integration.
approaches.example: Millions of vectors, filtered search, a strict latency budget.

approaches.name: An embedded, in-process library
approaches.what: A library that runs inside your application and stores its index on local disk.
approaches.greatWhen: Data is small to medium, the app is a single process, and cost matters most.
approaches.avoidWhen: Multiple app servers need to share one live, frequently updated index.
approaches.example: A prototype serving from one server, with no separate service to run.

approaches.name: A self-hosted search engine with vector support
approaches.what: Run your own cluster of a search engine that also supports vector search.
approaches.greatWhen: The team already operates a search cluster and wants full control.
approaches.avoidWhen: Nobody on the team is available to operate the cluster.
approaches.example: The same cluster already used for full-text search and logs.

approaches.name: Re-embed on every request instead of storing vectors
approaches.what: Skip storage entirely and recompute embeddings each time they're needed.
approaches.avoidWhen: Always, once the same content is searched more than once.
approaches.example: Every query recomputes embeddings for the whole library, wasting time and money.

challenge.question: You already run a relational database for orders and customers. Your RAG system has 50,000 chunks and moderate query volume. Where should embeddings live first?

options.text: Add a vector index to the database you already run
options.why: Fewer moving parts, one backup and access path, plenty for this scale. You can migrate later with real evidence.
It will work, but adds a new vendor, connection and bill before there's evidence you need its extra scale.

options.text: An embedded library on a single server
options.why: Multiple app servers can't reliably share one on-disk index, and updates can be lost across restarts.

options.text: Re-embed every document on every request
options.why: Wastes money and time recomputing something that should be stored once.

bestCase.title: Start with what you run, migrate only with evidence
bestCase.example: The team adds a vector index next to the existing tables, ships in a week, and only evaluates a dedicated vector service a year later when query volume grows 20x and filtered search gets slow.

worstCase.title: A new vendor before there's a real need
worstCase.example: The team adopts a dedicated vector service on day one for a 50,000-chunk dataset, spends two sprints wiring a new connection, auth and monitoring, and pays for capacity it uses a tenth of.

route.travelling: 50,000 help-center chunks, needing a home for their vectors

steps.label: Check what you already run
steps.goes: The team already operates a relational database with spare capacity.
steps.goesWrong: The team skips this check and starts evaluating vendors first.

steps.label: Add a vector index there
steps.goes: One migration, one connection, indexes built in minutes.

steps.label: Load test at real volume
steps.goes: Latency stays inside budget at expected traffic.

steps.label: Set a re-check trigger
steps.goes: The team agrees to reconsider only if volume or latency crosses a stated line.

takeaway: Start vector storage with what you already operate; move to a dedicated service only when a real number proves you've outgrown it.
